paper_metadata.title: Effect of μ-phase precipitation on the microstructural evolution and tensile properties of non-equiatomic CoCrFeNiMo medium-entropy alloys

The further addition of Mo also facilitates the formation of μ phase and greatly hardens the Mo7.5 alloy without accompanying serious embrittlement.

The ingots with nominal compositions of Co 17.5Cr12.5Fe55Ni10Mo5 and Co 18Cr12.5Fe55Ni7Mo7.5 were casted in a vacuum induction melting equipment (MC100V, Indutherm, Walzbachtal-Wossingen, Germany) under an Ar atmosphere using pure metals (purity higher than 99.9%).
The obtained rectangular ingots with the dimensions of 100 × 35 × 8 mm3 were homogenized at 1250 °C for 6 h, pickled in a 20% HCl to remove scales and contaminants, and milled to a thickness of 7 mm.

parameters.deformation: ~79% thickness reduction, from 7 mm to 1.5 mm

evidence.quote: For further grain refinement, the pickled ingots were rolled at room temperature with a thickness reduction ratio of ~79% (from 7 to 1.5 mm).
The rolled sheets were annealed at temperatures in the range between 900 and 1200 °C for 60 min, and subsequently water-quenched.

In the Mo5 alloy, the peaks of the specimens annealed above 1000 °C indicate a single fcc crystal structure, while the diffraction peaks of the second phase along with fcc peaks are observed in the specimen annealed at 900 °C.

attributes.location: grain boundaries and within fcc grains

evidence.quote: The specimen annealed at 900 °C exhibits submicron m-phase particles precipitated at grain boundaries and within fcc grains, as confirmed from the XRD and TEM results.
From the XRD and TEM analyses, the introduced alloys are composed of fcc and μ phase.

Meanwhile, only the specimen annealed at 1200 °C maintained a single fcc phase in the Mo7.5 alloy. When annealed at 900-1100 °C, the specimens contained peaks not only corresponding to the fcc phase but also the m phase.

evidence.quote: The EDS elemental mapping and chemical composition of each constituent phase reveal that they are enriched with Mo, and agree well with the calculated equilibrium composition of each phase. These results suggest that this is an Mo-rich m phase. It can be seen that the m phase formed mainly at grain boundaries, and secondarily within fcc grains.
The μ phase is found to be a Mo-rich phase. The microstructural evolution shows that the further addition of Mo enhances the formation of μ phase.

The formation of m phase effectively enhances the strength of the Mo7.5 alloy by precipitation strengthening

The hardness of the μ-phase particles is extremely high in the order of 15 GPa. These hard particles precipitated at boundaries and those in the ductile fcc matrix are not plastically sheared by gliding dislocation during plastic deformation. Thus, they act as a strong barrier for dislocation motion, leading to the precipitation strengthening.

in addition to solid solution strengthening of alloys

We attribute this to the enhanced solid solution strengthening by further addition of Mo content in the Mo7.5 alloy. Mo has the largest metallic radius among the five elements in the present alloy system, and it is known that the increase in the Mo content in the fcc phase leads to the enhanced solid solution strengthening effect

Possible strengthening mechanisms responsible for the increase in the strength by varying annealing temperatures are divided into four: solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, grain-boundary strengthening, and dislocation strengthening.
In addition, grain-refinement with decreasing annealing temperature also enhances the strength of the material.
